passages.text: Concealed semantic and episodic autobiographical memory electrified

Electrophysiology-based concealed information tests (CIT) try to determine whether somebody possesses concealed information about a crime-related item (probe) by comparing event-related potentials (ERPs) between this item and comparison items (irrelevants). <sentence_start/>Although the broader field is sometimes referred to as “memory detection,” little attention has been paid to the precise type of underlying memory involved. <sentence_start/>This study begins addressing this issue by examining the key distinction between semantic and episodic memory in the autobiographical domain within a CIT paradigm. <sentence_start/>This study also addresses the issue of whether multiple repetitions of the items over the course of the session habituate the brain responses. <sentence_start/>Participants were tested in a 3-stimulus CIT with semantic autobiographical probes (their own date of birth) and episodic autobiographical probes (a secret date learned just before the study). <sentence_start/>Results dissociated these two memory conditions on several ERP components. <sentence_start/>Semantic probes elicited a smaller frontal N2 than episodic probes, consistent with the idea that the frontal N2 decreases with greater pre-existing knowledge about the item. <sentence_start/>Likewise, semantic probes elicited a smaller central N400 than episodic probes. <sentence_start/>Semantic probes also elicited a larger P3b than episodic probes because of their richer meaning. <sentence_start/>In contrast, episodic probes elicited a larger late positive complex (LPC) than semantic probes, because of the recent episodic memory associated with them. <sentence_start/>All these ERPs showed a difference between probes and irrelevants in both memory conditions, except for the N400, which showed a difference only in the semantic condition. <sentence_start/>Finally, although repetition affected the ERPs, it did not reduce the difference between probes and irrelevants. <sentence_start/>These findings show that the type of memory associated with a probe has both theoretical and practical importance for CIT research.
Introduction

The logic of concealed information tests (CIT) is that stimuli that are known or familiar to people should elicit a different response relative to comparable stimuli that are new (Lykken, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B42" count="1">1959</citation>). <sentence_start/>Such tests could have various forensic applications, for example, to determine whether a person who denies having information about certain crime details or certain sensitive information actually possesses such information. <sentence_start/>CITs have been studied for many decades using several dependent variables, including long-standing, peripheral psychophysiological measures (Ben-Shakhar and Elaad, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B7" pmid="12675401" doi="10.1037/0021-9010.88.1.131" count="1">2003</citation>) and, more recently, electrophysiological (event-related potential, ERP) (Rosenfeld et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B69" pmid="3209369" doi="10.3109/00207458808985770" count="1">1988</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B67" pmid="1946897" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1991.tb02202.x" count="1">1991</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B70" doi="10.1016/j.physbeh.2009.03.030" pmid="18823418" count="1">2008</citation>; Farwell and Donchin, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B16" pmid="1758929" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1991.tb01990.x" count="1">1991</citation>; Allen et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B1" pmid="1410180" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1992.tb02024.x" count="1">1992</citation>) and hemodynamic ones (functional magnetic resonance imaging, fMRI) (Langleben et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B40" doi="10.1006/nimg.2001.1003" pmid="11848716" count="1">2002</citation>; Phan et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B58" doi="10.1016/j.acra.2004.11.023" pmid="15721593" count="1">2005</citation>; Christ et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B10" doi="10.1093/cercor/bhn189" pmid="18980948" pmcid="PMC2693617" count="1">2009</citation>; Nose et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B52" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2008.11.002" pmid="19059486" count="1">2009</citation>; Ganis et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B24" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2010.11.025" pmid="21111834" count="1">2011</citation>).

ERP-based CITs have garnered increased attention lately due to several advantages (e.g., Rosenfeld et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B70" doi="10.1016/j.physbeh.2009.03.030" pmid="18823418" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>(1) They have shown high accuracy rates reliably in detecting concealed information in mock crime scenario paradigms, at least in the laboratory conditions tested. <sentence_start/>(2) They are relatively inexpensive to implement. <sentence_start/>(3) The data can be acquired relatively quickly by using a few recording sites on the head. <sentence_start/>However, the underlying neural mechanisms are largely undetermined. <sentence_start/>A critical, understudied issue in the field is that people can learn and remember information about an event in many ways.

For example, memory theories distinguish between semantic and episodic memory (Tulving, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B89" count="1">1972</citation>), and different brain systems have been implicated in each. <sentence_start/>Episodic memory depends on mediotemporal lobe structures, especially the hippocampus, whereas semantic memory does so much less, if at all, and depends on association cortex, such as anterior temporal cortex (Vargha-Khadem et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B94" doi="10.1126/science.277.5324.376" pmid="9219696" count="1">1997</citation>; Schmolck et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B80" doi="10.1002/hipo.10039" pmid="12201637" count="1">2002</citation>; Eichenbaum et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B15" doi="10.1146/annurev.neuro.30.051606.094328" pmid="17417939" pmcid="PMC2064941" count="1">2007</citation>; Patterson et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B57" doi="10.1038/nrn2277" pmid="18026167" count="1">2007</citation>; Bayley et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B5" doi="10.1002/hipo.20417" pmid="18306299" pmcid="PMC2515556" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>That different brain systems support episodic and semantic memory raises the important issue that the brain signatures should differ when concealed information revealed on a CIT relies to different degrees on episodic vs. semantic memory. <sentence_start/>For example, evidence from developmental amnesia patients, who have hippocampal damage and impaired episodic but spared semantic memory, suggests that even residual hippocampal function (despite 50% volume loss or more) is necessary and sufficient to support relative sparing of the ability to imagine false events (Maguire et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B43" doi="10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2010.06.037" pmid="20603137" pmcid="PMC2937213" count="1">2010</citation>), which is a necessary episodic memory ability for effective deception; neural signatures of such hippocampal activity would thus be expected to be greater for a CIT based on episodic memory relative to one based on semantic memory.

Indeed, the episodic-semantic distinction extends also to the kind of autobiographical memory typically tested in CITs (e.g., Martinelli et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B45" doi="10.1002/hbm.22008" pmid="22359397" pmcid="PMC6870171" count="1">2012</citation>), the focus of this paper. <sentence_start/>There are episodic and semantic forms of autobiographical memory. <sentence_start/>An episodic memory encompasses concrete and unique details associated with distinct events that were experienced by a person in a specific spatiotemporal context and, critically, becomes an episodic autobiographical memory (EAM) when this memory also refers to the self in relation to that context (Tulving, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B91" doi="10.1146/annurev.psych.53.100901.135114" pmid="11752477" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>For example, details about a specific experience that happened at a certain time and place that caught one by surprise. <sentence_start/>In contrast, semantic autobiographical memory (SAM) encompasses personal information, including general knowledge of personal facts not associated with a specific time and place of acquisition (e.g., “my name is Pat” or “my birthday is December 5th”) and non-specific events, including both repeated and extended events (e.g., schema and script knowledge about “birthdays” not associated with any specific time and place, such as that birthdays are fun and involve friends and family) (Schank and Abelson, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B75" count="1">1977</citation>). <sentence_start/>Studies in neurological patients confirm this distinction. <sentence_start/>For example, amnesic patient K.C. (Tulving, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B90" count="1">1993</citation>) could report semantic knowledge, such as his own date of birth, but not any autobiographical episodic information (e.g., autobiographical details about any specific birthday). <sentence_start/>An important question is whether autobiographical probes associated with high semantic vs. episodic memory are associated with different neural processes in the context of a CIT, as would be predicted by neurocognitive studies of these two types of memories (e.g., Tulving et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B92" pmid="3166816" doi="10.1016/0278-2626(88)90035-8" count="1">1988</citation>; Martinelli et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B45" doi="10.1002/hbm.22008" pmid="22359397" pmcid="PMC6870171" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>This question also has applied relevance because it could provide information about the brain signatures of these different types of memories that can inform how to maximize detecting concealed information in specific cases. <sentence_start/>It is important to note that, although there may be distinct neural systems supporting EAM and SAM (e.g., Martinelli et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B45" doi="10.1002/hbm.22008" pmid="22359397" pmcid="PMC6870171" count="1">2012</citation>), most information in real life is often associated with both EAM and SAM, though with different relative strengths. <sentence_start/>Note that, for simplicity, in the rest of the paper we will often omit the attribute “autobiographical” and refer simply to semantic and episodic memory.

The main previous ERP study that addressed a related question with an explicitly applied focus is one by Rosenfeld et al. (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B68" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2005.06.002" pmid="16137781" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>“High-impact” and “low-impact” probes were compared that differed in semantic and episodic memory content. <sentence_start/>The high-impact probe was the participant's name, whereas the low-impact probe was the experimenter's name (i.e., “JULIE”). <sentence_start/>The ERP differences between high-impact probes and a set of random control names (referred to as “irrelevants” in the CIT literature) were much larger than those between the low-impact probes and the irrelevants (i.e., the CIT effect was larger for high than low-impact probes). <sentence_start/>However, important issues about this finding need to be resolved. <sentence_start/>First, the same low-impact probe was used for all participants (i.e., the experimenter's name was always “JULIE”). <sentence_start/>This raises the concern that there could be something intrinsically special, and consistently so across participants, about this name (e.g., frequency, length, associations). <sentence_start/>This confound was not present for the high-impact probes, as they varied across participants. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, it is unclear whether the female name used for everybody in the low-impact condition might have been processed differently by male and female participants (i.e., Julie is a female name), as well as individuals (i.e., different people named Julie that each one knows), increasing variability in the results. <sentence_start/>The ERPs were also recorded from only three sites, limiting assessment of spatial distribution differences between conditions. <sentence_start/>Finally, the study examined only the P3, leaving it open what effects other ERPs might show, such as the centroparietal N400 marker of semantic memory (Kutas and Federmeier, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B38" doi="10.1146/annurev.psych.093008.131123" pmid="20809790" pmcid="PMC4052444" count="1">2011</citation>) or the parietal late positive complex (LPC) associated with episodic recollection (Rugg and Curran, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B72" doi="10.1016/j.tics.2007.04.004" pmid="17481940" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>We would argue that the better way to describe the high- and low-impact probes is in terms of how they activate different kinds of memory. <sentence_start/>For example, both probes activate semantic and episodic memory, but in different ways for the participant's name (“high-impact”) and the experimenter's name (“low-impact”). <sentence_start/>Specifically, the participant's name could activate semantic memory more automatically than episodic memory, on average, because people are overlearned experts at responding to their own name, whereas most episodic memories associated with their name would be remote and many would be highly similar and so not distinctly memorable, such as people calling their name, potentially resulting in a lot of interference for recalling associated episodic memories and making them effortful to activate (Soderlund et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B84" doi="10.1002/hipo.20927" pmid="21404363" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Thus, semantic memory would be exceptionally automatic for the participant's name, consistent with evidence for a large auditory N400 for one's own name relative to other proper names and no evidence for a posterior LPC effect, suggesting little difference in episodic memory for one's own name and other proper names (Muller and Kutas, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B50" pmid="9051785" doi="10.1097/00001756-199612200-00045" count="1">1996</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, by telling subjects that the experimenter's name is “Julie,” subjects acquire a recent episodic memory, which is less effortful to activate than the more remote memories associated with one's own name (Soderlund et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B84" doi="10.1002/hipo.20927" pmid="21404363" count="1">2012</citation>), predicting a larger LPC for the experimenter's than participant's name, but this has not yet been examined to date. <sentence_start/>In summary, we would suggest that in the study by Rosenfeld et al. (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B68" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2005.06.002" pmid="16137781" count="1">2006</citation>), the participant's name would predominantly activate SAM, whereas the experimenter's name would predominantly activate recent EAM, but such ideas have not yet been systematically addressed.

Thus, the first goal of the current study was to address the question of concealed information based on different types of memory more directly while getting around the limitations in the previous work. <sentence_start/>First, comparable stimuli without a gender component were used for the semantic (the participant's date of birth) and episodic (a “secret” date given to the participant just before the study) autobiographical memory conditions. <sentence_start/>Second, all probes and irrelevants varied by person, eliminating any systematic biases in the group average. <sentence_start/>Third, 32 recording sites were used, enabling potential scalp distribution differences in the ERPs elicited by the two conditions to be determined. <sentence_start/>Fourth, and related to the previous point, not only the P3 but also other ERPs were evaluated, including the frontal N2, the N400, and the LPC.

A second important issue that has not been addressed systematically in the ERP literature is the effect of stimulus repetition. <sentence_start/>Because of the relatively low signal-to-noise ratio achievable with all behavioral and psychophysiological measures employed, the typical CIT paradigm averages several tens of trials in which probes and irrelevants repeat many times. <sentence_start/>Differences between probes and irrelevants using psychophysiological measures, such as skin conductance, decrease rapidly with stimulus repetition because of habituation (e.g., Ben-Shakhar et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B8" pmid="1153633" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1975.tb01291.x" count="1">1975</citation>; Ben-Shakhar and Elaad, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B6" pmid="12395821" doi="10.1037/0021-9010.87.5.972" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, the same effect may not be present with ERP measures because they may tap into different mechanisms. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, potential differences between semantic and episodic probes may change over the course of the experimental session. <sentence_start/>For example, repeated presentation will reactivate semantic and/or episodic memories associated with a probe but do less so if at all for irrelevants, since no distinct semantic or episodic information is available about them. <sentence_start/>This could result in a difference between probes and irrelevants that becomes larger over time, as ERP repetition effects can be greater for meaningful than meaningless items (Schendan and Maher, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B78" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2008.09.061" pmid="19010426" count="1">2009</citation>; Voss et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B100" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.09.012" pmid="19770053" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Another possibility is that repetition of the probes might alter the activation of the semantic and/or episodic memory underlying each. <sentence_start/>For example, the episodic probe might develop increasing associations with the experimental context, resulting in development of semantic memory (Gratton et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B27" doi="10.3758/MC.37.3.277" pmid="19246343" pmcid="PMC2682721" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>This might reduce the N400 (which is smaller when semantic memory activates more successfully) (Voss et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B100" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.09.012" pmid="19770053" count="1">2010</citation>; Voss and Federmeier, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B97" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2010.01085.x" pmid="20701709" pmcid="PMC2982896" count="1">2011</citation>), thereby reducing differences between semantic and episodic probes. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, all stimuli, including the semantic probe, might develop additional episodic memories with each exposure in the experiment, resulting in additional episodic memories that might increase the LPC (which is larger for more episodic memory), thereby also reducing differences between semantic and episodic probes and associated CIT effects.

The key idea in classical CIT theories is that probes will generate an orienting response associated with, for example, increased skin conductance (e.g., Sokolov, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B85" doi="10.1146/annurev.ph.25.030163.002553" pmid="13977960" count="1">1963</citation>; Gati and Ben-Shakhar, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B25" pmid="2145391" doi="10.1037//0096-3445.119.3.251" count="1">1990</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although these theories may be adequate to explain autonomic nervous system findings, they cover only a subset of the central nervous system processes engaged by a probe during the CIT (relative to irrelevants) and implicitly assume that probes activate only one kind of memory. <sentence_start/>However, in the framework described here, semantic and episodic probes may be associated with different neural processes.

Current theories of memory predict that semantic probes would primarily activate semantic memories stored in the neocortex and indexed by ERPs such as the N400 and P3b, whereas episodic probes would primarily activate episodic memory stored in mediotemporal and linked cortical structures, indexed by late parietal potentials, such as the LPC (Paller and Kutas, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B53" doi="10.1162/jocn.1992.4.4.375" pmid="23968130" count="1">1992</citation>; Rugg et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B73" doi="10.1038/33396" pmid="9560154" count="1">1998</citation>; Dien et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B13" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2004.00193.x" pmid="15318873" count="1">2004</citation>; Voss and Paller, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B99" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3931-05.2006" pmid="16421312" pmcid="PMC6675383" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>In practice, most stimuli are associated with both semantic and episodic memories, and so they would elicit some combination of these effects. <sentence_start/>For the stimuli in this study, one's date of birth is associated with strong SAM, activating meaning-related processes about oneself in semantic memory but also activating episodic memories incidentally (e.g., events during a specific birthday party, although this may be reduced by providing only the day and month of each date). <sentence_start/>Prior to the experiment, the birth date is also associated with relatively remote episodic memories of birthday events and other experiences involving one's birth date, such as filling out applications (e.g., for jobs, insurance, taxes). <sentence_start/>In addition, as the birth date is repeatedly experienced over the course of the experiment, each of these experiences may be encoded as a new (1) episodic memory (Paller and Wagner, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B56" doi="10.1016/S1364-6613(00)01845-3" pmid="15866193" count="1">2002</citation>) and/or (2) constructed memory that combines new and old (i.e., due to incidental recollection of various birth date memories) episodic elements as well as semantic memory (Hassabis and Maguire, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B29" doi="10.1098/rstb.2008.0296" pmid="19528007" pmcid="PMC2666702" count="1">2009</citation>).

New, recent episodic memory encoding can also occur for a different date with no semantic or episodic memory associated with it before the experiment, such as the secret date. <sentence_start/>Importantly, while multiple trace theory proposes that the hippocampus supports all episodic memories, regardless of how long ago they were encoded (Nadel et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B51" doi="10.1002/1098-1063(2000)10:4<352::AID-HIPO2>3.0.CO;2-D" pmid="10985275" count="1">2000</citation>), some evidence suggests that different parts of the hippocampus support more recent vs. remote episodic memory (Kesner and Hunsaker, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B36" doi="10.1016/j.bbr.2009.12.029" pmid="20036694" count="1">2010</citation>; Mankin et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B44" doi="10.1073/pnas.1214107109" pmid="23132944" pmcid="PMC3511087" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Further, between 3 days and 3 months after the learning episode, episodic memories may become semantic by increasing connectivity between cortical areas while decreasing connectivity with the hippocampus (Harand et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B28" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0043495" pmid="22937055" pmcid="PMC3427359" count="1">2012</citation>), and a study comparing episodic memories for events ranging in time from very recent (3-14 days old) to very remote (10 years old) found evidence that the hippocampus and the EAM cortical network are integrated more strongly for recent than remote memories (Soderlund et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B84" doi="10.1002/hipo.20927" pmid="21404363" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Consequently, more remote memories require more strategic top-down processes in prefrontal cortex for them to be retrieved than do more recent memories. <sentence_start/>This predicts that ERP effects related to EAM will be greater for the secret date, which involves very recent episodic memory, than the birth date, which involves mostly much more remote episodic memory.

On the other hand, the secret date is minimally meaningful (i.e., low in semantic memory) relative to the birth date. <sentence_start/>Repeated experiences with any date could potentially begin to construct new semantic memory about that date (Curran et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B12" pmid="12452581" doi="10.3758/cabn.2.1.1" count="1">2002</citation>; Gratton et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B27" doi="10.3758/MC.37.3.277" pmid="19246343" pmcid="PMC2682721" count="1">2009</citation>), but the ability to do so would be minimal because little meaningful information is provided about any dates within the experiment. <sentence_start/>Notably, the information that the probe is a secret date to be kept concealed during the experiment is meaningful and could lead to learning this as new semantic memory due to repeated experiences with it; knowledge and semantic memory typically require multiple experiences to acquire (Glisky and Schacter, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B26" count="1">1987</citation>; Verfaellie and Cermak, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B95" pmid="7924352" doi="10.1016/s0010-9452(13)80200-6" count="1">1994</citation>). <sentence_start/>Another important way that all these semantic and episodic memory processes could affect the CIT is by inducing standard oddball effects thought to be related to ongoing contextual updating processes in working memory (Kutas et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B39" doi="10.1126/science.887923" pmid="887923" count="1">1977</citation>; Donchin and Coles, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B14" count="1">1988</citation>; Dien et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B13" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2004.00193.x" pmid="15318873" count="1">2004</citation>; Polich, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B62" doi="10.1016/j.clinph.2007.04.019" pmid="17573239" pmcid="PMC2715154" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>This could result in a larger P3b to the probes than irrelevants. <sentence_start/>Further, the P3b to probe conditions could differ as a function of the relative combination of associated semantic and episodic memory. <sentence_start/>In sum, the birth date potentially activates a combination of high semantic memory and remote episodic memory for multiple birthdays related events, whereas the secret date potentially activates a combination of low semantic memory and recent episodic memory for a single event. <sentence_start/>Despite reflecting a combination of memory influences, the birthdate and secret date provide an interesting and important starting point for assessing the role of semantic and episodic memory in CITs.

The focus of this paper is on the frontal N2, N400, P3, and LPC components. <sentence_start/>The frontal N2 is important because recent studies suggest that concealed information in CITs modulate this component with visual (Gamer and Berti, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B21" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2009.00933.x" pmid="20003148" count="1">2010</citation>) and auditory stimuli (Matsuda et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B46" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2009.07.004" pmid="19631702" count="1">2009</citation>), with probes eliciting a larger frontal N2 than irrelevants. <sentence_start/>This would be predicted by orienting reflex theory (Ben-Shakhar and Elaad, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B7" pmid="12675401" doi="10.1037/0021-9010.88.1.131" count="1">2003</citation>), as the probe is more meaningful than the irrelevants and occurs infrequently (it is “novel” within the local stimulus sequence). <sentence_start/>If the frontal N2 reflects primarily an orienting reflex to meaningful information, the N2 should be larger for (1) probes and targets than irrelevants, and (2) semantic autobiographical information, such as one's date of birth, relative to recently acquired episodic information, such as a random (secret) date seen just before the study. <sentence_start/>However, the frontal N2 is known to be modulated by other variables as well, including the extent to which a stimulus matches to memory (e.g., Folstein and Van Petten, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B18" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2007.00602.x" pmid="17850238" pmcid="PMC2365910" count="1">2008</citation>; Folstein et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B19" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2007.00628.x" pmid="18047482" pmcid="PMC2386436" count="1">2008</citation>): the less a stimulus matches memory, the larger the N2. <sentence_start/>The precise type of memory involved is usually not specified, but knowledge (e.g., of an object category) and working memory have been mainly studied so far. <sentence_start/>Thus, an alternative prediction can be made based on the idea that match to knowledge is relevant for N2 modulation. <sentence_start/>The numbers and month abbreviations used as stimuli will activate knowledge about numbers and months, respectively. <sentence_start/>This predicts that the N2 will be larger to the irrelevants (minimal memory: people have minimal knowledge about the numbers in random dates that have no task relevance) than a meaningful item (e.g., birth date with rich semantic and remote episodic memories). <sentence_start/>In addition, depending upon how much new memory is encoded for the episodic item (e.g., a “secret” probe date will be associated with new episodic memory and possibly new knowledge induced by repetition within the experimental context), the N2 to this item may be in-between that to irrelevants and the semantic item.

The centroparietal N400 is larger when an item activates semantic memory less relative to more successfully (Kutas and Federmeier, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B38" doi="10.1146/annurev.psych.093008.131123" pmid="20809790" pmcid="PMC4052444" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although people know the numbers and month abbreviations used to denote dates, an arbitrary date is not very rich in meaning. <sentence_start/>In contrast, one's birth date is personally meaningful because it is rich in SAM. <sentence_start/>This predicts that the N400 will be larger for irrelevant dates than the semantic item (birthdate). <sentence_start/>In addition, as with the frontal N2, depending upon the extent to which new semantic memory is encoded for the episodic item, its N400 may be in-between that to irrelevants and the semantic item. <sentence_start/>However, the N2, which merely requires new knowledge to be acquired, may be more sensitive to the memory manipulations in this experiment than the N400, which requires the more demanding encoding of a meaningful representation. <sentence_start/>After all, the episodic manipulation can induce new knowledge to be learned, but this new information is minimal in meaning, and meaningful representations would typically require a stronger induction event than that used in this experiment (Gratton et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B27" doi="10.3758/MC.37.3.277" pmid="19246343" pmcid="PMC2682721" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>For example, acquisition of category knowledge with minimal associated meaning modulates a frontocentral N2 but not necessarily the N400 (Folstein et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B19" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2007.00628.x" pmid="18047482" pmcid="PMC2386436" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>The N400 may thus show little or no difference between irrelevants and episodic items, instead differing primarily between irrelevants and semantic items.

The effect of concealed information on the P3 has been investigated in numerous ERP studies (e.g., Rosenfeld et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B69" pmid="3209369" doi="10.3109/00207458808985770" count="1">1988</citation>; Allen et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B1" pmid="1410180" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1992.tb02024.x" count="1">1992</citation>; Rosenfeld et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B71" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2004.00158.x" pmid="15032986" count="1">2004</citation>), but almost all used fewer than five recording sites and so differences between the spatial distribution of the P3 in the different conditions may have been missed. <sentence_start/>Indeed, the P3 is a family of components, and what has usually been referred to as P3 in previous studies is most likely an instance of the P3b, which has been dissociated from the P3a (Dien et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B13" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2004.00193.x" pmid="15318873" count="1">2004</citation>; Polich, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B62" doi="10.1016/j.clinph.2007.04.019" pmid="17573239" pmcid="PMC2715154" count="1">2007</citation>; Verleger, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B96" doi="10.1016/j.clinph.2007.11.175" pmid="18222107" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>The P3b is known to be modulated by many factors, including the subjective probability of items in a perceived category, the complexity of the task and stimuli, and stimulus value (e.g., Johnson, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B31" pmid="3774922" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1986.tb00649.x" count="1">1986</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B32" pmid="8416066" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1993.tb03208.x" count="1">1993</citation>). <sentence_start/>We predicted that the P3b to probes would be larger than to irrelevants, replicating previous findings (e.g., Rosenfeld et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B71" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2004.00158.x" pmid="15032986" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>Further, the semantic probes might elicit a larger P3b than the episodic probes in part because they were the only items associated with strong semantic memory and so they may stand out more in the stream of irrelevants, which are associated only with episodic information acquired during the study.

Finally, the LPC is typically larger during tasks that entail the reactivation of episodic memories (Rugg and Curran, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B72" doi="10.1016/j.tics.2007.04.004" pmid="17481940" count="1">2007</citation>) and so we expected the LPC to be larger to probes, for which episodic memories have been clearly associated, than to irrelevants, for which episodic memory is minimal, and larger to probes in the episodic than semantic condition.
Materials and methods
Subjects

Twenty-five naïve healthy volunteers (18 females, between 18 and 35 years of age, mean = 21, <italic>SD</italic> = 3.5 average age: <italic>z</italic> years), recruited from the University of Plymouth (UoP), took part in for course credit. <sentence_start/>Data from eight participants were excluded due to excessive artifacts (7) or failure to carry out the task as instructed (1). <sentence_start/>Participants had normal or corrected vision, and no history of neurological or psychiatric disease. <sentence_start/>All procedures were approved by the UoP Ethics Board.
Stimuli

The stimuli were dates in the format “day month” (e.g., 15 Apr, Figure 1) commonly used by our European participants, subtending about 3 × 2° of visual angle. <sentence_start/>Three types of dates were used in each condition: irrelevants, probe, and target. <sentence_start/>During the week preceding the study, at the same time detailed and demographics and health questionnaires were administered, participants were asked over the phone to provide their own date of birth (only the day and month were required) and a list of other important dates (dates of birth of close relatives and friends, anniversaries and so on), so that a set of irrelevant dates could be generated for each participant that excludes these personally important dates. <sentence_start/>For the semantic autobiographical condition, the probe was the birth date of each participant. <sentence_start/>For the episodic autobiographical condition, the probe was a date that differed from all other dates used in the study and was not on the participant's list of important dates. <sentence_start/>The irrelevant dates used for the episodic and semantic conditions were always different. <sentence_start/>Irrelevant dates never shared the day or the month of the probe or target dates, and they were never famous dates. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, the target never shared the day or month of the probe.
Figure 1

<bold>Schematic of the experimental paradigm.</bold> <sentence_start/>Participants were tested in two memory conditions in separate blocks: semantic autobiographical and episodic autobiographical. <sentence_start/>In both conditions, they saw four irrelevant dates, randomly intermixed with a target date and a probe date. <sentence_start/>In the semantic autobiographical condition, the probe was the participant's date of birth. <sentence_start/>In the episodic autobiographical condition, it was a secret date in an envelope each participant opened just before the study. <sentence_start/>Participants reported whether they possessed associated memories for any of the dates, responding honestly to both the irrelevant dates (by pressing the “no” key) and the target date (by pressing the “yes” key), but lying about their birth date or secret date (by pressing the “no” key). <sentence_start/>Note: Item type labels in the figure shown for illustration only and did not appear on the stimuli.
Procedure

Before beginning the EEG setup, participants were shown a target date and then were unexpectedly taken into an adjacent fire refuge area by an assistant and the experimenter and they were given an envelope containing their “secret” date. <sentence_start/>Next, the experimenter left the room, and participants were told by the assistant to open the envelope and to memorize the secret date contained in it, ensuring not to do anything that could reveal they knew this date to the experimenter. <sentence_start/>Participants were also told that this was their own secret date, different from everyone else's, and that they should keep the note it was written on in their pocket or purse. <sentence_start/>After setting up the EEG cap and electrodes, participants were seated on a comfortable chair in front of a computer screen (about 114 cm away) in a dark room. <sentence_start/>Two conditions were administered in separate blocks, the semantic and episodic conditions, with order counterbalanced across participants. <sentence_start/>In the semantic condition, the probe date was the individual's birth date whereas, in the episodic condition, it was the “secret date.” <sentence_start/>This secret date varied by participant to match the between-participant variability of the date of birth. <sentence_start/>In both semantic and episodic conditions, participants were instructed to deny possessing any memory for the probe date (birth date or secret date, respectively) throughout the session by giving a deceptive “no” response. <sentence_start/>They were also instructed to give an honest “yes” response about knowing the target date. <sentence_start/>Thus, participants had to report honestly whether they knew each date, but they had to lie about the probe date. <sentence_start/>In sum, participants responded honestly to both the target (pressing “yes”) and the irrelevants (pressing “no”) but deceptively to the probe (pressing “no”). <sentence_start/>Participants responded by pressing one of two buttons with the index and middle finger of their dominant hand. <sentence_start/>They were instructed to respond as fast as possible without sacrificing accuracy. <sentence_start/>Each item was presented for 800 ms with an inter-trial interval of 3000 ms. <sentence_start/>In each condition, each item (four irrelevants, one probe, and one target) was presented 35 times in a pseudo-random order for a total of 210 trials. <sentence_start/>The constraints on the pseudo-random sequence were that a probe and a target could never appear in temporally adjacent trials, and any individual irrelevant could only repeat for a maximum of three times in the sequence. <sentence_start/>The same abstract sequence (i.e., the sequence of irrelevant, probe and target types of items) was used for the two conditions to eliminate potential differences due to sequence statistics. <sentence_start/>Each condition was split into two blocks of ~7 min each, to test the effect of stimulus repetition. <sentence_start/>There was a short practice session (10 trials) before the experimental trials. <sentence_start/>Finally, at the end of the study, participants were asked to recall the target and the secret dates and indicate if they had any pre-experiment memory associated with any of the other dates. <sentence_start/>Since there was 100% recall accuracy in all cases, the recall data were not further analyzed.
Electrophysiological data acquisition

The electroencephalogram (EEG) was sampled at 250 Hz from Ag/AgCl electrodes (gain = 20,000, bandpass filtering = 0.01-100 Hz). <sentence_start/>EEG data were collected from 32 electrodes arranged in a geodesic array (Figure 3) and additional electrodes placed below the right eye referenced to left mastoid to monitor eye blinks, on the tip of the nose, and the right mastoid, all of which were referenced to the left mastoid. <sentence_start/>Note that in this configuration, Fz is just posterior to site 27, Cz coincides with site 28, and Pz is just posterior to site 29. <sentence_start/>Horizontal eye movements were monitored using two electrodes placed on the outer canthi of the right and left eyes, referenced to each other. <sentence_start/>Electrode impedance was below 5 kΩ for all channels.
Analyses

Performance measures were submitted to ANOVAs with three factors: item type (average of irrelevants; probe; target), memory condition (semantic and episodic), and repetition (first and second half). <sentence_start/>To ensure participants carried out the task, follow-up ANOVAs also contrasted targets with irrelevants and targets with probes. <sentence_start/>However, the main comparison of interest for each memory condition was between probes and irrelevants because the same response (“no”) was associated with both. <sentence_start/>As this comparison was the main focus of this experiment, and targets received a different response (“yes”) from all other items, confounding their comparison with other items, ERP analyses focus only on an item factor that include probes and irrelevants; note, preliminary analyses that included ERPs to the targets confirms expected target P3b effects. <sentence_start/>In the following, significant differences between probes and irrelevants (in the behavioral or ERP data) will be referred to as the CIT effect.
Response times
Response times (RTs) and accuracy rates were analyzed in the omnibus ANOVA and planned comparisons.
ERPs

ERPs were averaged off-line for an epoch of 1000 ms, including a 100 ms baseline. <sentence_start/>Trials affected by blinks, eye movements, muscle activity or amplifier blocking were rejected off-line. <sentence_start/>An average of 31 artifact-free trials per item type per participant went into the analyses (<italic>MIN</italic> = 16, <italic>SD</italic> = 4.2). <sentence_start/>A One-Way ANOVA showed no differences in the number of trials across conditions (including both repetitions), <italic>F</italic><sub>(5, 85)</sub> = 1.05, <italic>p</italic> > 0.1, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.06. <sentence_start/>Data were analyzed unfiltered but shown filtered at low-pass 30 Hz in the figures. <sentence_start/>Repeated measures ANOVAs on the mean amplitude of the average ERPs assessed the effects of item type and condition on the N2, N400, P3, and LPC components. <sentence_start/>The time windows used for the main analyses centered arounds the mean peak latency of the N2 (250-350 ms), the N400 (350-500 ms), the P3 (400-600 ms), and the LPC (750-900 ms). <sentence_start/>To assess the overall pattern of results, a “lateral” ANOVA assessed lateral sites (13 pairs, see electrode montage in Figure 3) using factors of Item Type (probes vs. irrelevants), Site, and Hemisphere. <sentence_start/>A second, “midline” ANOVA assessed the midline sites (six electrodes) using factors of Item Type and Site.

Planned focal analyses were also conducted at frontal sites 1 and 2 for the N2, central site 28 (Cz) for the N400, and parietal site 30 for the P3b and LPC, where these components were maximal. <sentence_start/>These analyses compared (1) probes and irrelevants (i.e., the CIT effect) in both memory conditions, since we predicted differences between probes and irrelevants in both cases, and (2) probes between the two conditions, since we predicted differences between the semantic and episodic probes. <sentence_start/>Note that we did not carry out amplitude-latency analyses on the P3b because the overlapping N400 made it difficult to determine P3b peak latency in single participants. <sentence_start/>The focal analysis was carried out on the mean amplitude data within the time windows used in the main analyses. <sentence_start/>At focal sites, onset of the CIT effect (i.e., probes vs. irrelevants) and the difference between semantic and episodic probes was determined. <sentence_start/>For the N2 and N400, 25 ms time windows were used, between 100 ms and 350 ms, and 300 and 550 ms, respectively. <sentence_start/>A paired <italic>t</italic>-test between the conditions of interest was carried out on each time window until a significant difference was found in three successive time windows. <sentence_start/>The time window preceding the first significant time window was used as an estimate of the onset time of the effect. <sentence_start/>For the P3, the same logic was used with 25 ms time windows between 200 and 600 ms.

Event-related potentials (ERPs)

Qualitatively, the ERP waveform showed an occipitotemporal P1 and a corresponding anterior N1, followed by a frontocentral P2 and N2, and a centroparietal N400, P3b, and LPC (Figures 3-7). <sentence_start/>Four main differences between items and memory conditions are evident in the ERPs. <sentence_start/>The first difference is on the N2, maximal at frontal sites between 250 and 350 ms (Figures 3, 4 and 5A). <sentence_start/>Second, a clear N400 component overlapping the first part of the P3b is present in the episodic condition, maximal at central sites, and to a lesser extent in the semantic condition (Figures 3 and 5B). <sentence_start/>The third difference is on the P3b, maximal at centroparietal sites between 400 and 600 ms (Figures 4 and 5C). <sentence_start/>Fourth, LPC differences appear later at the same sites, lasting until the end of the epoch (Figures 4 and 5C). <sentence_start/>Omnibus statistics are shown in Tables 1-3 and described below.

Planned focal analyses on frontal pair 1 and 2 showed that probes were more positive than irrelevants (4.35 vs. 2.10 μV, respectively), <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 40.01, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.71, and this CIT effect tended to be larger on the right than the left (3.46 vs. 2.99 μV, respectively), <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 4.01, <italic>p</italic> = 0.063, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.20. <sentence_start/>Importantly, this CIT effect was larger in the semantic than episodic condition, <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 5.53, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.26, due to the probes in the semantic condition being more positive than those in the episodic condition (4.87 vs. 3.83 μV, respectively), <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 4.50, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.22. <sentence_start/>This result is the opposite of the hypothesis that the N2 CIT effects reflect orienting to novelty but consistent with the alternative hypothesis that the N2 is sensitive to match to knowledge. <sentence_start/>No repetition effects were significant.

The onset of the CIT effect in the two memory conditions was determined at right frontal site 2, where the differences were largest. <sentence_start/>Results showed that the CIT effect onset between 200 and 225 ms in the semantic probe condition, and slightly later, between 225 and 250 ms, in the episodic probe condition. <sentence_start/>A second onset analysis showed that the onset of the difference between probes in the two memory conditions was also between 225 and 250 ms.

<bold><italic>N400.</italic></bold> <sentence_start/>The N400 is the only ERP component to show a CIT effect only in the semantic condition. <sentence_start/>The N400 is smallest for the semantic probe, relative to the episodic probe and all irrelevants, which are indistinguishable from each other (Figure 3). <sentence_start/>Figure 4 (middle) shows an overall centroparietal scalp distribution between 400 and 600 ms due to the combination of the central CIT effect on the earlier N400 and the parietal CIT effect on the later P3b. <sentence_start/>Figure 5B shows the memory effect around central sites where the N400 overlaps least with the frontal N2 and parietal P3b, illustrating that the N400 is more negative to episodic than semantic probes and has a central maximum and overall centroparietal scalp distribution, which is characteristic of the N400 index of semantic memory (Kutas and Federmeier, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B38" doi="10.1146/annurev.psych.093008.131123" pmid="20809790" pmcid="PMC4052444" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>The omnibus analyses on the N2 and P3b capture the early and late part of the N400, so the focus was on planned focal analyses.

A focal analysis on Cz (site 28) showed that probes were less negative than irrelevants (7.29 vs. 5.16 μV, respectively), <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 7.05, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.31, and this effect was larger in the semantic than episodic condition (3.27 vs. 0.96 μV, respectively), <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 6.16, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.28. <sentence_start/>A follow-up analysis showed that the difference between probes and irrelevants was only significant in the semantic condition, <italic>t</italic><sub>(16)</sub> > 2.35, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05, for both repetitions. <sentence_start/>ERPs were more positive during the second than first repetition, <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 4.58, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.22, but this effect did not interact with any other factors. <sentence_start/>Finally, ERPs were more positive during the semantic than episodic conditions, <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 8.73, <italic>p</italic> < 0.01, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.35.

Finally, an onset analysis of the CIT effect in both memory conditions was carried out at Cz. <sentence_start/>Results showed that the CIT effect onset between 400 and 425 ms in the semantic conditions, whereas it onset between 475 and 500 ms in the episodic condition. <sentence_start/>A second onset analysis showed that the onset of the difference between probes in the two memory conditions was between 400 and 425 ms.

Omnibus results (Table 2) showed a larger P3b for probes than irrelevants at lateral (I, 6.84 vs. 4.30 μV, respectively) and midline sites. <sentence_start/>This CIT effect was maximal at lateral and midline centroparietal sites (I × S), and lateral results showed that this effect was larger on the right at frontocentral sites but on the left at more posterior sites (I × S × H). <sentence_start/>Importantly, the difference between probes and irrelevants was larger in the semantic than episodic condition at lateral and midline sites (M × I), and this interaction was largest at centroparietal sites (lateral, M × I × S). <sentence_start/>ERPs at this time tended to be more positive during the second than the first half (<italic>R</italic>). <sentence_start/>At lateral sites, this repetition effect was larger on the right at frontal and posterior sites, but symmetrical at central sites, and maximal at right centroparietal sites (R × S × H). <sentence_start/>The lateral repetition effect was also modulated by item type, as it was larger for probes than irrelevants (I × R × S × H), and by memory type, as it was larger at centroparietal sites in the semantic condition, but at fronto-central sites in the episodic condition (M × R × S).

Planned focal analyses were conducted at parietal site 30 where the P3b was maximal. <sentence_start/>Consistent with the omnibus analysis, the P3b was larger for probes than irrelevants, <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 38.35, <italic>p</italic> < 0.001, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.71 (10.77 vs. 7.15 μV, respectively). <sentence_start/>Importantly, this CIT effect was larger in the semantic than episodic condition, <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 5.26, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.25 (4.80 vs. 2.45 μV, respectively) because the P3b was more positive for the semantic than episodic probes, <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 4.53, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.22 (11.84 vs. 9.7 μV, respectively). <sentence_start/>There was a non-significant trend for the P3b to be larger during the second than the first half, <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 3.56, <italic>p</italic> = 0.08, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.18, and the CIT effect was numerically larger during the second than the first half, but this interaction of item and repetition was also not significant, <italic>F</italic><sub>(1, 16)</sub> = 2.47, <italic>p</italic> = 0.14, η<sup>2</sup> = 0.13 (4.11 vs. 3.14 μV, respectively). <sentence_start/>Thus, the CIT effect did not change significantly as a function of repetition (if anything, it became slightly larger).
