Discussion

In summary, performance is consistent with previous CIT studies using the 3-stimulus paradigm with speeded responses in that responses for probes and targets are slower and less accurate than for irrelevants (e.g., Gamer et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B20" doi="10.1002/hbm.20343" pmid="17290371" pmcid="PMC6871443" count="1">2007</citation>; Gamer and Berti, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B21" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2009.00933.x" pmid="20003148" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>The present results also provide evidence for repetition priming, as responses to all items are faster in the second than the first half of each memory condition block, on average. <sentence_start/>ERPs show multiple effects. <sentence_start/>First, the frontal N2 is larger to irrelevants than both types of probes, and the CIT effect on the N2 starts by 225 ms in the semantic condition but slightly later, by 250 ms, in the episodic condition. <sentence_start/>Second, semantic and episodic probes begin to be processed differently by 250 ms, and this early effect is maximal at frontal sites, where the N2 is larger for episodic than semantic probes. <sentence_start/>Third, the N400 shows a CIT effect only in the semantic condition, as a central N400 is smaller for the semantic probe relative to the episodic probe and irrelevants, which resemble each other. <sentence_start/>Fourth, probes generate a larger P3b than irrelevants, and this CIT effect starts by 400 ms and is larger for semantic than episodic probes. <sentence_start/>Fifth, episodic probes generate a larger LPC than semantic probes. <sentence_start/>Sixth, although ERPs became more positive in the second half of the trials, the CIT effect on the P3b remains similar. <sentence_start/>Next, we discuss these findings in turn.
Performance

The behavioral results indicate that probes and targets are more difficult to process than irrelevants. <sentence_start/>The typical explanation for this finding is that both infrequent probes and targets stand out in the stream of irrelevants but require different responses. <sentence_start/>This creates a conflict that takes some time to resolve (Gamer et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B20" doi="10.1002/hbm.20343" pmid="17290371" pmcid="PMC6871443" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Note that, since targets were the only items requiring a “yes” response, the direct comparison between targets and irrelevant is not very informative. <sentence_start/>The pattern of behavioral effects was the same for both memory conditions. <sentence_start/>This indicates that the ERP differences between these conditions do not reflect RT or accuracy differences, and suggests that the probes in these two conditions were similar in terms of saliency. <sentence_start/>The overall repetition effect on the RTs, but the lack of a repetition effect on the difference between probes and irrelevants, indicates that repetition had mostly a generic effect independent of item type.
Frontal N2 and centroparietal N400: knowledge and semantic memory
N2

At least two types of frontal N2 components have been distinguished, a cognitive control N2 and a memory (mis)match N2, whose amplitude is modulated by different factors (Folstein and Van Petten, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B18" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2007.00602.x" pmid="17850238" pmcid="PMC2365910" count="1">2008</citation>; Folstein et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B19" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2007.00628.x" pmid="18047482" pmcid="PMC2386436" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Concealed information studies have focused on the cognitive control N2 and most used an orienting reflex account. <sentence_start/>Clearly, the pattern of effects on the frontal N2 found here is not consistent with a simple orienting reflex explanation (Sokolov, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B85" doi="10.1146/annurev.ph.25.030163.002553" pmid="13977960" count="1">1963</citation>). <sentence_start/>The N2 is largest for the frequent irrelevants which, according to an orienting reflex account, should be the least salient stimuli and so should be associated instead with the smallest N2.

Most previous CIT studies using ERPs have focused exclusively on the P3b component, making it difficult to compare our results with those of the previous literature. <sentence_start/>More troublesome, the low-pass filtering employed in some studies is so extreme (around 4 Hz in some cases) that any effects on fast changing components like the frontal N2 would be wiped out (Rosenfeld et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B68" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2005.06.002" pmid="16137781" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, two recent CIT studies examined the effect of the experimental manipulations on components of the N2-family (Matsuda et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B46" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2009.07.004" pmid="19631702" count="1">2009</citation>; Gamer and Berti, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B21" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2009.00933.x" pmid="20003148" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>The study by Matsuda and collaborators used a 2-stimulus paradigm (i.e., no targets were present), auditory stimuli of an episodic nature (single digits), long interstimulus intervals (22 s) to enable peripheral psychophysiological recordings, and a common average reference montage, making it difficult to compare the results with those of the current study with visual stimuli, fast intertrial intervals, and average mastoid reference. <sentence_start/>Their findings showed a slightly larger central N2 for probes than irrelevants, which the authors suggest is an N2b reflecting the redirection of attentional resources to salient stimuli (Matsuda et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B46" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2009.07.004" pmid="19631702" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>The study by Gamer and Berti (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B21" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2009.00933.x" pmid="20003148" count="1">2010</citation>) is perhaps more comparable to the present study since it employed visual stimuli, a 3-stimulus paradigm, and a right mastoid reference. <sentence_start/>This study reported a larger frontal N2 to probes than irrelevants, and attributed such an effect to cognitive control processes required for response monitoring. <sentence_start/>Such an explanation would predict a larger frontal N2 for probes than irrelevants in the current study as well, but the opposite was found. <sentence_start/>It is possible that differences in the paradigms could account for this discrepancy: The stimuli differed (playing cards were used in that study compared to dates here), different interstimulus intervals were used (8 s, on average in that study vs. 2 s here), and stimuli were not counterbalanced across participants in the earlier work, leaving open the possibility of item-specific confounds. <sentence_start/>These differences in the paradigm clearly resulted in ERP differences compared with standard CIT results as, for example, there was no P3b effect. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, a subsequent CIT study by the same group (Gamer and Berti, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B22" doi="10.3389/fnhum.2012.00308" pmid="23162454" pmcid="PMC3498630" count="1">2012</citation>) failed to find any N2 effects. <sentence_start/>Although further work is required to fully characterize the factors that affect the frontal N2 in CIT paradigms, the current study shows that concealed information is not necessarily associated with a larger frontal N2 in CIT paradigms and that the literature is inconsistent.

The pattern of N2 effects suggests that the degree to which an item matches memory, a factor known to modulate frontal N2 amplitude (i.e., larger N2 for memory mismatch), is the key factor modulating the N2 in this study. <sentence_start/>This interpretation is supported by the finding that the frontal N2 is smaller for the date of birth, the item associated with the most semantic (and remote episodic) memory, followed by the secret date, which is associated with recent episodic memory for the learning experience in which the participant received the envelope with this date (and perhaps some newly acquired semantic memory, e.g., the fact that the date is a secret), and by the irrelevants, which have very little associated semantic or episodic memory. <sentence_start/>Based on this finding alone, we cannot rule out that this N2 effect reflects both semantic and episodic memory, but prior evidence implicates semantic memory more. <sentence_start/>The N2 memory match effect has primarily been found when knowledge is manipulated, not in episodic memory experiments. <sentence_start/>This knowledge is not necessarily semantic (meaning) <italic>per se</italic>, because frontal effects, especially frontopolar ones where the N2 is maximum here, are not always found with semantic manipulations (Ganis and Kutas, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B23" doi="10.1016/S0926-6410(02)00244-6" pmid="12668221" count="1">2003</citation>; Kutas and Federmeier, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B38" doi="10.1146/annurev.psych.093008.131123" pmid="20809790" pmcid="PMC4052444" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>A visual knowledge interpretation is also indicated by evidence that a frontal N3(00) complex from 200 to 500 ms, which includes the memory match N2 as an early component of this waveform, is specific to processing visual images (Barrett and Rugg, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B3" pmid="2771030" doi="10.1016/0028-3932(89)90067-5" count="1">1989</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B4" pmid="2285513" doi="10.1016/0278-2626(90)90029-n" count="1">1990</citation>; McPherson and Holcomb, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B47" pmid="10098380" doi="10.1017/s0048577299971196" count="1">1999</citation>) and modulated according to how successfully visual knowledge is activated for a category decision (e.g., dog, cat, car) (Schendan and Kutas, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B76" doi="10.1016/S0028-3932(01)00176-2" pmid="11900745" count="1">2002</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B77" doi="10.1162/089892903321107864" pmid="12590847" count="1">2003</citation>; Schendan and Maher, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B78" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2008.09.061" pmid="19010426" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Finally, it is noteworthy that ERPs in the N2 time window became more positive with repetition, but the effect did not vary by item type. <sentence_start/>Such an increase over multiple repetitions may reflect accumulation of knowledge with each repetition, as in category learning, which can modulate the frontal N2, the N400, and other ERPs (Curran et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B12" pmid="12452581" doi="10.3758/cabn.2.1.1" count="1">2002</citation>; Folstein and Van Petten, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B17" doi="10.1037/0278-7393.30.5.1026" pmid="15355134" count="1">2004</citation>; Folstein et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B19" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2007.00628.x" pmid="18047482" pmcid="PMC2386436" count="1">2008</citation>; Scott et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B82" doi="10.1016/j.brainres.2008.02.054" pmid="18417106" count="1">2008</citation>; Gratton et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B27" doi="10.3758/MC.37.3.277" pmid="19246343" pmcid="PMC2682721" count="1">2009</citation>).

This interpretation of the N2 is consistent with the modulation of the N400 index of semantic memory, which is clearest at central sites [see site C<italic>z</italic>(28) in Figure 5B] where the N400 overlaps least with the frontal N2 and the parietal P3b. <sentence_start/>The N400 is more negative for episodic than semantic probes because the amplitude of the N400 is inversely proportional to the amount of semantic memory associated with both linguistic and non-linguistic stimuli (e.g., Kutas and Federmeier, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B38" doi="10.1146/annurev.psych.093008.131123" pmid="20809790" pmcid="PMC4052444" count="1">2011</citation>): A secret random date acquired just before the study has little or no semantic memory associated with it, compared to one's birth date, which is by far the most meaningful stimulus. <sentence_start/>Consequently, meaning activates most successfully for this semantic probe, and its N400 is smallest. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the N400 is larger to the episodic probe (secret date), but comparably as large to the irrelevants. <sentence_start/>The similarity between the N400 to the episodic probe and the irrelevants is consistent with the fact that the meanings of all these items are minimal and about the same (i.e., just the meaning of the numbers and months but no other richly meaningful facts). <sentence_start/>This also indicates that the new information about the secret date acquired before the study did not result in a sufficiently meaningful representation to affect the semantic memory processes underlying the N400. <sentence_start/>Notably, in contrast, the secret date information did result in new knowledge, such as visual knowledge, as demonstrated by the smaller frontal N2 for the episodic probe relative to the irrelevants. <sentence_start/>This is consistent with evidence that certain types of newly acquired knowledge result in sensitivity of the frontal N2 (and similar frontal negativities between 200 and 500 ms, e.g., frontal N3 complex, N300, N350, N390 components) to this knowledge (Curran et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B12" pmid="12452581" doi="10.3758/cabn.2.1.1" count="1">2002</citation>; Ganis and Kutas, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B23" doi="10.1016/S0926-6410(02)00244-6" pmid="12668221" count="1">2003</citation>; Folstein and Van Petten, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B17" doi="10.1037/0278-7393.30.5.1026" pmid="15355134" count="1">2004</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B18" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2007.00602.x" pmid="17850238" pmcid="PMC2365910" count="1">2008</citation>; Folstein et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B19" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2007.00628.x" pmid="18047482" pmcid="PMC2386436" count="1">2008</citation>; Schendan and Maher, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B78" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2008.09.061" pmid="19010426" count="1">2009</citation>), but additional more richly meaningful information needs to be provided for the centroparietal N400 to become sensitive to newly acquired facts about an item (Gratton et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B27" doi="10.3758/MC.37.3.277" pmid="19246343" pmcid="PMC2682721" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Importantly for deception detection, this means that the N400 shows a CIT effect for semantic autobiographical information, and quite a robust one, but minimal to no CIT effect for episodic autobiographical information.

Previous CIT studies have not reported N400 effects for several reasons. <sentence_start/>First, the N400 effect is largest at Cz(28) but overlaps to some extent the P3b spatiotemporally at this site and parietal sites. <sentence_start/>A number of CIT studies have used only the three midline sites Pz, Cz, and Fz, or reported data only for those sites (e.g., Rosenfeld et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B69" pmid="3209369" doi="10.3109/00207458808985770" count="1">1988</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B71" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2004.00158.x" pmid="15032986" count="1">2004</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B68" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2005.06.002" pmid="16137781" count="1">2006</citation>; Gamer and Berti, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B21" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2009.00933.x" pmid="20003148" count="1">2010</citation>), and so may have missed N400 effects or analyzed them as part of the P3b effects. <sentence_start/>Second, as mentioned in the context of the frontal N2, extreme low-pass filtering to enhance slow components like the P3b might have spuriously reduced effects on faster-varying components such as the N400 (e.g., Rosenfeld et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B68" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2005.06.002" pmid="16137781" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>A third reason is suggested by the present finding of a CIT effect on the N400 only in the semantic condition. <sentence_start/>Episodic stimuli do not show a CIT effect because, in the present work and many previous studies, they do not have sufficiently rich semantic memory representations to produce a CIT effect on the N400.

From a memory perspective, it is necessary to consider the alternative that the frontal N2 and centroparietal N400 effects reflect instead episodic memory. <sentence_start/>Indeed, frontal negativity between 100 and 300 ms (during the N2) does show memory effects, being more negative for new than old items during recognition tasks (Tsivilis et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B88" pmid="11516405" doi="10.1016/s0896-6273(01)00376-2" count="1">2001</citation>), but the interpretation of such repetition effects, and similar ones on the N400, is controversial (Rugg and Curran, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B72" doi="10.1016/j.tics.2007.04.004" pmid="17481940" count="1">2007</citation>) and, if anything, points to knowledge, conceptual memory, and semantic memory (Paller et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B55" doi="10.1016/j.tics.2007.04.002" pmid="17475539" count="1">2007</citation>; Voss et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B100" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.09.012" pmid="19770053" count="1">2010</citation>; Voss and Federmeier, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B97" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2010.01085.x" pmid="20701709" pmcid="PMC2982896" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>These issues have been discussed in detail in the debate about whether an N400-like component, which sometimes appears to have a more frontal (and so labeled “FN400”) than centroparietal distribution, reflects episodic familiarity or conceptual implicit memory (due to activation of meaning representations) (Paller et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B55" doi="10.1016/j.tics.2007.04.002" pmid="17475539" count="1">2007</citation>; Rugg and Curran, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B72" doi="10.1016/j.tics.2007.04.004" pmid="17481940" count="1">2007</citation>; Voss and Federmeier, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B97" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2010.01085.x" pmid="20701709" pmcid="PMC2982896" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>While this debate is beyond the scope of this paper, it is relevant to consider whether the frontal N2 or N400 pattern might reflect episodic familiarity. <sentence_start/>We suggest that familiarity can't simply or easily explain the N400. <sentence_start/>First, one might argue that the semantic probe (one's birthday) has more lifetime familiarity than the episodic probe (an arbitrary date with no other meaning) because episodic memories set up prior to the EEG recording are numerous (albeit more remote) for one's birthday but only singular (albeit more recent) for the episodic probe. <sentence_start/>These pre-existing episodic memories for one's birthday therefore reduce the N400 (or N2) for the semantic more than the episodic probe. <sentence_start/>Second, both semantic and episodic probes are equally as familiar in terms of exposure during EEG recording (i.e., repeated the same number of times), which is the typical way that episodic familiarity is defined experimentally. <sentence_start/>This predicts no difference between semantic and episodic probes, in contrast to the clear memory effects observed. <sentence_start/>Third, connectivity between the hippocampus and neocortex is stronger for recent episodic memory, which is the kind primarily associated with the episodic probe, relative to remote episodic memory, which is only associated with the semantic probe (Soderlund et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B84" doi="10.1002/hipo.20927" pmid="21404363" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Such differential hippocampal-cortical linkages would predict a greater reduction in episodic memory-related cortical activity for the episodic than semantic probe, thereby resulting in a smaller N400 (or N2) for the episodic than semantic probe-the opposite of the observed pattern. <sentence_start/>Fourth, altogether, these episodic memory considerations would predict a larger N400 for the irrelevants than the episodic probe because the episodic probe was studied beforehand but the irrelevants were not (and so are less familiar), but no evidence was found for any difference between the episodic probe and irrelevants. <sentence_start/>The parsimonious explanation is that the consolidated semantic memory in the cortex for the semantic probe drives the N400 pattern, as argued here. <sentence_start/>Consistent with this, the FN400 has been argued to be identical to the N400 and to reflect semantic memory and conceptual implicit memory for repeated items (Paller et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B55" doi="10.1016/j.tics.2007.04.002" pmid="17475539" count="1">2007</citation>; Voss et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B100" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.09.012" pmid="19770053" count="1">2010</citation>; Voss and Federmeier, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B97" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2010.01085.x" pmid="20701709" pmcid="PMC2982896" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Note, as all items repeated here many times, conceptual priming (due to conceptual implicit memory) could explain the N400 pattern, not only semantic memory (Renoult and Debruille, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B64" doi="10.1162/jocn.2009.21410" pmid="19929764" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>The N400 shows robust modulation with conceptual priming, being smaller for repeated than new meaningful items (Paller et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B55" doi="10.1016/j.tics.2007.04.002" pmid="17475539" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Conceptual priming would be greater for the meaningful semantic probe than the minimally meaningful episodic probe (Voss et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B100" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.09.012" pmid="19770053" count="1">2010</citation>), consistent with the observed pattern.

Together, these findings suggest that the N2 and N400, as highly sensitive markers of knowledge and semantic memory, respectively, could potentially be used for detecting concealed information, but only if the type of memory is considered carefully and the concealed information that one is trying to detect is stored in the brain systems for knowledge and semantic memory. <sentence_start/>In contrast, if the goal is to detect episodic memory, then later brain potentials, like the P3b and LPC, may be more suitable markers. <sentence_start/>In most realistic cases, in which the probes are associated with both semantic and episodic memory, both types of markers should be considered.
P3b

The main prior study that addressed an issue similar to the one addressed here is the one by Rosenfeld and Collaborators (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B68" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2005.06.002" pmid="16137781" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>The relevant finding from that study is that the P3b difference between probes and irrelevants was much smaller for low-impact probes (the recently learned experimenter's name) than high-impact probes (a participant's name). <sentence_start/>In fact, the difference between probes and irrelevants in the low-impact condition was close to zero. <sentence_start/>Like that study, we found that semantic probes elicit a larger P3b than episodic ones: The CIT effect is larger in the semantic than episodic condition. <sentence_start/>Even so, at least in the analysis within a fixed P3b window, episodic probes show a sizeable CIT effect on the P3b. <sentence_start/>One possible explanation for this discrepancy is that, in the prior study, the low-impact probes were incidentally learned, even though they were encountered numerous times in the experiment. <sentence_start/>In the current study, participants were explicitly told that the (episodic) probe was a secret date that they had to lie about. <sentence_start/>This constitutes intentional encoding, which results in greater episodic memory than incidental encoding and likely also increases the saliency of such a date (Hyde and Jenkins, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B30" count="1">1973</citation>; Craik and Tulving, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B11" count="1">1975</citation>; Kellogg et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B35" pmid="7137417" count="1">1982</citation>). <sentence_start/>Given the intentional nature of deception, intentional study would also be expected to transfer more appropriately to the intentional retrieval situation of the CIT paradigm than incidental study (Tulving and Thomson, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B93" count="1">1973</citation>; Morris et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B48" count="1">1977</citation>). <sentence_start/>Since the stimulus sequences used in the two memory conditions were identical, this finding confirms that the P3b is modulated by the type of memory triggered by the probe, not just by context updating taking place in working memory (Johnson, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B31" pmid="3774922" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1986.tb00649.x" count="1">1986</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B32" pmid="8416066" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1993.tb03208.x" count="1">1993</citation>). <sentence_start/>Importantly, the CIT effect on the P3b did not become smaller with repetition, but rather, tended to become larger. <sentence_start/>This indicates that the duration of the test is not a major issue in P3-based CITs, and the benefit of longer ERP sessions with more trials may not be cancelled by habituation effects, as usually seen with electrodermal measures (Ben-Shakhar et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B8" pmid="1153633" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.1975.tb01291.x" count="1">1975</citation>). <sentence_start/>Future work will have to determine whether the CIT effect on the P3b is constant for even longer sessions that may be required in the field. <sentence_start/>It is noteworthy that our results may underestimate the size of the P3b in the episodic condition during its initial phase when it overlaps the N400 at central sites due to the opposing polarities of these ERPs (Figures 3-5), but not afterwards around the P3b peak and thereafter from 500 to 600 ms.

The P3b pattern bolsters the interpretation of the earlier frontal N2 and centroparietal N400 patterns in terms of knowledge and semantic memory. <sentence_start/>Both the present findings and the Rosenfeld et al. (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B68" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2005.06.002" pmid="16137781" count="1">2006</citation>) study indicate that the CIT effect on the P3b is larger for semantic items (e.g., your own birth date and name, respectively) relative to items that are less meaningful or about which one has less knowledge (e.g., a secret date, irrelevants). <sentence_start/>Likewise, in experiments on semantic memory using an object categorization task, a parietal P3b-like component, peaking around 600 ms, is more positive for objects categorized more than less successfully (Schendan and Kutas, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B76" doi="10.1016/S0028-3932(01)00176-2" pmid="11900745" count="1">2002</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B77" doi="10.1162/089892903321107864" pmid="12590847" count="1">2003</citation>; Schendan and Maher, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B78" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2008.09.061" pmid="19010426" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Consequently, in the present study, the P3b is larger for the semantic than episodic probe possibly because subjects more successfully identify the semantic probe as their birthdate relative to the episodic probe as the secret date and discriminate the semantic better than the episodic probe from the irrelevant dates in order to generate a deceptive response; after all, the episodic probe and the irrelevants have minimal to no meaning and so they may be less discriminable from each other in terms of knowledge and semantic memory. <sentence_start/>Altogether, the N2, N400, and P3b all point to the importance of knowledge and semantic memory for demonstrating a CIT effect on these ERPs.
LPC

Even though previous CIT studies have considered episodic memory, no previous ERP study has examined specifically the LPC, which is well established as a marker of conscious recollection from episodic memory (Paller and Kutas, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B53" doi="10.1162/jocn.1992.4.4.375" pmid="23968130" count="1">1992</citation>; Rugg and Curran, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B72" doi="10.1016/j.tics.2007.04.004" pmid="17481940" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the present study, episodic probes elicit a larger LPC than semantic ones. <sentence_start/>This finding is consistent with studies of episodic memory in which people decide whether an item is new or old (e.g., Paller et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B54" count="1">1995</citation>). <sentence_start/>In these studies, a larger LPC is typically found for old items recognized as such (e.g., items with associated episodic knowledge) relative to new items. <sentence_start/>The parietal distribution and time course of this old/new LPC resembles the LPC memory effect found here. <sentence_start/>The present LPC finding thus indicates that, when the concealed information is thought to be primarily or predominantly due to episodic memory, then the LPC may be the most robust ERP to examine in CIT paradigms. <sentence_start/>Intriguingly, the LPC pattern is the only ERP finding that parallels the RT pattern: The LPC is more positive and RTs are slower for episodic than semantic probes, which are slower than irrelevants. <sentence_start/>However, the LPC starts after the RTs in the episodic condition, on average, suggesting that the recollection process underlying the LPC cannot drive the RT effect.
Repetition

Repetition effects should be explored in future ERP work, especially given the sensitivity demonstrated here of RTs and accuracy to this factor. <sentence_start/>Overall, RTs and ERPs between 250 and 350 ms, 400 and 600 ms, and 750 and 900 ms show repetition effects, but focal analyses on the N2, N400, P3b, and LPC show no repetition effects, perhaps due to insufficient power. <sentence_start/>Intriguingly, RT repetition effects to all item types (i.e., faster responses in the second than first half) tend to be larger (albeit non-significantly) in the episodic than semantic condition. <sentence_start/>However, no ERP repetition effect is larger in the episodic than semantic condition, but given the weakness of the RT interaction, power may have been insufficient to detect this also in the ERPs. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, it appears that the N2 and N400 are larger for episodic than semantic in the first (Figure 6) more than the second half of trials (Figure 7), whereas the P3b is larger for semantic than episodic, and the LPC is larger for episodic than semantic in the second more than first half. <sentence_start/>Future ERP studies should manipulate repetition with a greater number of trials and in more subtle ways and evaluate whether repetition modulates the CIT effect on these ERPs and if so, how.
Performance and ERPs

RTs, accuracy, and ERP effects differed from each other so it is unclear which ERP effects drive the behavioral effects. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, a few points can be made. <sentence_start/>The LPC starts too late (after 700 ms) to drive RT effects (all faster than 700 ms, on average) and corresponding accuracy of these responses. <sentence_start/>The P3b (400-600 ms) overlaps the earliest RTs, which are to irrelevants (500-600 ms), and so is also probably too late to influence RTs to irrelevants and even too late to influence RTs to probes much if at all (600-700 ms). <sentence_start/>The N2 and N400 are thus the ERP markers that are most likely to be responsible for the RTs and corresponding accuracy. <sentence_start/>Consistent with this, the N2 has long been recognized as having a time course and relationship with RTs consistent with the underlying decision processes driving the RTs during discrimination tasks, such as the CIT, in part because the N2 is early enough to drive the RTs, whereas the P3 is often too late, and N2 latency is related to RTs (Ritter et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B66" doi="10.1126/science.424760" pmid="424760" count="1">1979</citation>). <sentence_start/>Likewise, the N3 complex, which includes the (mis)match N2, is related to RTs during category decisions (Philiastides and Sajda, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B60" doi="10.1093/cercor/bhi130" pmid="16014865" count="1">2006</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B61" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3540-07.2007" pmid="18045902" pmcid="PMC6673396" count="1">2007</citation>; Philiastides et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B59" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1655-06.2006" pmid="16943552" pmcid="PMC6675324" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Given that both the N2 and N400 show a CIT effect in the semantic condition, the RT CIT effect in this condition could reflect both knowledge and semantic memory processes underlying these ERPs. <sentence_start/>Given that the N2 but not the N400 shows a CIT effect in both the semantic and episodic conditions, the knowledge processes underlying the N2 but not the N400 drives the CIT effect in the episodic condition. <sentence_start/>However, it is likely that at least the initial CIT effect on the P3b, which starts within 400 ms in the semantic condition and within 475 ms in the episodic condition, could further influence the RTs. <sentence_start/>However, the finding that P3b CIT effects end around 650 ms, which is after the response to all items except the episodic probe in the first half of trials suggests that the processes underlying the P3b are unlikely to be the only factor influencing behavior. <sentence_start/>This highlights the importance of considering the (mis)match frontal N2 and N400 and underlying knowledge and semantic memory processes, respectively, in future CIT studies and for deception detection, in general.
Saliency and related factors

Memories can differ in saliency, but how they differ depends upon many factors. <sentence_start/>Manipulating these factors was beyond the scope of this initial experiment but will be important for future research. <sentence_start/>We highlight here a few key issues regarding saliency and memory. <sentence_start/>First, saliency needs to be defined clearly but as yet a good definition is lacking, in general and in the memory field. <sentence_start/>Saliency has been most clearly defined in the context of selective attention to perceptual information. <sentence_start/>In particular, saliency is defined operationally by search performance: Items that differ along certain perceptual dimensions from the surrounding context are more salient and can be detected faster than items that do not differ as much from the surrounding context (e.g., a red dot against a background of green distractor dots). <sentence_start/>Saliency so defined orients selective attention, which can occur in parallel in early visual areas (Treisman, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B87" doi="10.1080/13506280500195250" pmid="17387378" pmcid="PMC1832144" count="1">2006</citation>) and, after the initial separation of stimulus information into features, binds these features together into an object representation and searches a scene serially (Wolfe et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B102" pmid="2527952" doi="10.1037//0096-1523.15.3.419" count="1">1989</citation>; Treisman, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B87" doi="10.1080/13506280500195250" pmid="17387378" pmcid="PMC1832144" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Depending upon the context and task goals, these computations can inform the selective attention system to attend to salient features (e.g., the red dot) and filter out distractors and less salient features (Kastner and Pinsk, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B33" pmid="15849892" doi="10.3758/cabn.4.4.483" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>Selective attention can also be driven endogenously (e.g., by task goals and memory), and the top-down feedback inputs that perform these functions proceed from higher to lower order areas of information processing (Buffalo et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B9" doi="10.1073/pnas.0907658106" pmid="20007766" pmcid="PMC2806732" count="1">2010</citation>).

Second, in CIT paradigms usually the various items do not differ perceptually and so “saliency” is driven entirely by stored memory and to its interaction with the details of the CIT paradigm. <sentence_start/>For example, probes and irrelevants are perceptually identical between conditions (i.e., all strings of two numbers and three letters) and have the same motor demands and so perceptual differences cannot drive saliency here: Saliency is determined primarily by memory. <sentence_start/>Notably, this dictates that, because memory is stored where it is processed in the cortex (Slotnick and Schacter, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B83" doi="10.1038/nn1252" pmid="15156146" count="1">2004</citation>; Schendan and Maher, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B78" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2008.09.061" pmid="19010426" count="1">2009</citation>), saliency effects might be observed at the same time as memory differences are computed and/or afterwards when an earlier memory computation influences later cognitive and other memory processes (Moses et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B49" doi="10.1016/j.brainresbull.2005.05.026" pmid="16140164" count="1">2005</citation>): Saliency effects can only be observed once the first memory effect has begun. <sentence_start/>Thus, it is necessary to consider how saliency has been defined in some of the few memory studies that have tried to address its role.

Third, in the memory field, definitions of saliency are based on memory representations, not perception, and differ between memory types: the information encoded in memory and its interactions with the task determine the salience of memory of a particular type (e.g., semantic or episodic), and such memory saliency computations can potentially influence another memory (of the same or a different type) activated simultaneously or later on in stimulus processing (e.g., semantic memory could influence episodic memory). <sentence_start/>For example, saliency of semantic memory has been defined based on (1) conceptual or perceptual distinctiveness in terms of dominance of meaning (e.g., for “bank,” the dominant meaning is associated with “money,” not “river”) (Rajaram, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B63" count="1">1998</citation>) or learned statistical regularities of the stimuli (e.g., orthographic frequency) (Rajaram, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B63" count="1">1998</citation>), respectively, or (2) the representation strength of semantic features (e.g., high visual vs. high motor) (Kellenbach et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B34" doi="10.1162/08989290260045819" pmid="12126498" count="1">2002</citation>; Koriat and Pearlman-Avnion, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B37" doi="10.1037/0096-3445.132.3.435" pmid="13678377" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>(3) For episodic memory, saliency (or significance) of autobiographical information is based on the personal relevance of the learning episode and is closely related to emotional salience (Westmacott and Moscovitch, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B101" pmid="12956240" doi="10.3758/bf03196114" count="1">2003</citation>), and this helps to preserve episodic memory (Levin et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B41" pmid="4009192" doi="10.1136/jnnp.48.6.556" pmcid="PMC1028372" count="1">1985</citation>) and semantic memory despite brain injury (Westmacott and Moscovitch, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B101" pmid="12956240" doi="10.3758/bf03196114" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>Note, by all these definitions, memory saliency is intrinsically entangled with the memory itself. <sentence_start/>On this basis, the birth date is higher in the saliency of both semantic and episodic memory than the secret date, predicting larger CIT effects across the entire ERP waveform. <sentence_start/>However, this was not the case because the LPC, consistent with this ERP as an index of episodic recollection, shows a larger CIT effect for the secret date. <sentence_start/>This raises the possibility that, for episodic memory, an additional definition of saliency is based on the role of recency (Soderlund et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B84" doi="10.1002/hipo.20927" pmid="21404363" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>The present findings suggest that episodic memory can be more salient when recent than remote, as the secret date was associated with more recent episodic memory than the birth date. <sentence_start/>Finally, these considerations and multiple memory systems theory (Schacter and Tulving, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B74" count="1">1994</citation>), more generally, highlight that saliency can only be defined within a particular type of memory; otherwise, one would be comparing apples and oranges. <sentence_start/>Saliency for semantic memory is not the same as saliency for episodic memory (e.g., meaning dominance determines salience for semantic memory vs. personal relevance determines salience for episodic memory). <sentence_start/>Thus, it would be difficult, if not theoretically impossible, to compare directly the saliency of items such as the birth and secret dates. <sentence_start/>For instance, on the one hand, it is uncommon to ask people explicitly to lie, and so the secret date has a very distinctive and salient episodic memory, and the recency of this memory may also enhance its saliency. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, the birth date usually has more personally relevant associated episodic memories than the secret date, and so it is very salient as well. <sentence_start/>In short, memory salience is greater for the birth date based on some definitions and memory types, whereas it is greater for the secret date based on others. <sentence_start/>Finally, we note that, by definition, semantic memory represents meaning, whereas episodic memory can store information regardless of meaning, as when people recognize non-sense visual patterns (Voss et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B98" doi="10.1093/cercor/bhr315" pmid="22079921" pmcid="PMC3432238" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Accordingly, the birth date is highly meaningful due to activating semantic memory, whereas the secret date is less meaningful due to activating semantic memory less successfully but instead activates episodic memory, due to its recency, more successfully than the birth date. <sentence_start/>Thus, as we argued, the birth and secret dates differ as a function of their ability to activate semantic or episodic memory, and differ in meaningfulness (as one definition of saliency) only as a function of the extent to which they activate semantic memory.

Fourth, saliency is not a property of an item alone but rather a property of the item in a particular context. <sentence_start/>For example, the frequent word “table” may be low in saliency when embedded in a list of other frequent words but highly salient in the context of famous names. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, memory saliency depends on the task at hand and can be modulated by attentional manipulations (Rajaram, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B63" count="1">1998</citation>), and so the word “table” can become highly salient in the context of other common words when the task requires detecting furniture words that appear infrequently. <sentence_start/>In the present CIT paradigm, the birth and secret dates occurred (in different blocks) infrequently within a stream of random dates, and they were the only items for which a lie had to be produced, making them highly salient in both conditions. <sentence_start/>The behavioral results support this and provide an operational definition of saliency for this task, as done in the attention field: faster RTs to probes are taken to reflect higher saliency in the task. <sentence_start/>Specifically, although RTs differ reliably between probes and irrelevants (documenting that the study had sufficient power to detect such differences), the memory conditions show no evidence of any difference that could be attributed to saliency. <sentence_start/>Thus, the CIT paradigm and procedures made both types of probes highly salient (being the only items for which a lie had to be produced) so that any residual saliency differences are very small; at most, probes show a non-significant trend to be faster in the semantic than episodic condition in the first block (596 vs. 640 ms). <sentence_start/>This could be due to the specific content of the memory (birthdate) or to the fact that the semantic probes were the only ones with a strong semantic content in the stream of irrelevants and targets (items with predominantly episodic memory associated with them and minimal semantic memory).

Finally, other reasons why we believe differential saliency was not an issue in the present study include the following. <sentence_start/>(1) If the birth date is more salient than the secret date, then a saliency-based account of the frontal N2 would predict a larger N2 to probes than irrelevants and a larger N2 for the birth than secret date. <sentence_start/>This is because, by definition, saliency engages attentional and other cognitive control processes (e.g., response monitoring, depending on the stimulus-response mapping) and these processes are typically associated with a larger N2 (Folstein and Van Petten, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B18" doi="10.1111/j.1469-8986.2007.00602.x" pmid="17850238" pmcid="PMC2365910" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>So, counterfactually, a smaller N2 for the date of birth than the secret date implies that date of birth was not more salient than the secret date. <sentence_start/>The same logic applies to the comparison between probes and irrelevants. <sentence_start/>Thus, the evidence is at odds with a saliency account and more in tune with a memory matching explanation. <sentence_start/>(2) Further, the LPC effect should be larger for the birth than the secret date, but the opposite was found, consistent with the idea that memory differences primarily drive the effects. <sentence_start/>(3) To our knowledge, there has been no systematic P300 CIT work suggesting that a recent memory leads to smaller P300s than one's birth date, unless such information is acquired incidentally (Rosenfeld et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B68" doi="10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2005.06.002" pmid="16137781" count="1">2006</citation>), which was not the case in our study, and no CIT studies have been conducted in which stimulus saliency was non-circularly defined and its systematic manipulation affected P300 amplitude (or any other ERP) in a way that could easily explain the current findings.
Memory task orientation

Memory is task-dependent; task instructions can influence the importance of a particular type of memory for performance and alter the pattern of effects (Richardson-Klavehn and Bjork, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B65" count="1">1988</citation>). <sentence_start/>Thus differential activation of semantic and episodic memory by the birth and secret dates may also change the memory orientation of the CIT task to favor semantic vs. episodic memory, respectively. <sentence_start/>Consider that a seemingly subtle difference in task instructions from categorization (e.g., categorize the object) to recognition (e.g., recognize the item as old or new) alters the cortical networks involved in processing the same item (Schendan and Stern, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B79" doi="10.1093/cercor/bhm197" pmid="18033768" count="1">2008</citation>), consistent with multiple memory system theory (Squire and Zola-Morgan, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B86" pmid="1896849" doi="10.1126/science.1896849" count="1">1991</citation>; Schacter and Tulving, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B74" count="1">1994</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the SAM condition, the task requirement to lie about the birthdate likely focuses attention on associated rich semantic memory and remote episodic memories because these memories distinguish the birth date from the target date and irrelevants. <sentence_start/>Likewise, in the EAM condition, the task requirement to lie about the secret date should instead focus attention on the one recent episodic memory to cue the task response, while also minimizing attention to any associated semantic memory or knowledge, because recent episodic memory most clearly distinguishes the secret date from the target date and irrelevants. <sentence_start/>Moreover, the EAM condition probably focuses attention on episodic memory more than the SAM condition because strategic retrieval processes in inferior prefrontal cortex are required more for remote than recent episodic recollection (Soderlund et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B84" doi="10.1002/hipo.20927" pmid="21404363" count="1">2012</citation>), and lying recruits such prefrontal processes to inhibit the prepotent truthful response. <sentence_start/>Altogether, this would make these neural resources less available to recollect episodic autobiographical memories, which is more of a problem for the birth date in the SAM condition where in these memories are more remote, than the EAM condition where in the memory is recent. <sentence_start/>Likewise, such prefrontal processes are also implicated in selecting episodic memory from competing alternatives (Badre and Wagner, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B2" doi="10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2007.06.015" pmid="17675110" count="1">2007</citation>), and the many remote episodic memories associated with the birthdate would require such selection processes more than the single recent episodic memory associated with the secret date. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the SAM condition orients the task predominantly toward using semantic memory as the primary cue to guide performance because semantic memory is retrieved more readily than is remote episodic memory. <sentence_start/>In contrast, the EAM condition orients the task predominantly toward recent episodic memory as the primary cue to guide performance. <sentence_start/>This predicts that the SAM condition should produce larger CIT effects on ERP components related to knowledge and semantic memory (i.e., N2, N400, and P3b), whereas the EAM condition should produce larger CIT effects on ERP components related to episodic memory (i.e., LPC), consistent with these findings. <sentence_start/>Such task orientation effects would then interact with the memory retrieved to determine task performance (Schyns, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B81" pmid="9735539" doi="10.1016/s0010-0277(98)00016-x" count="1">1998</citation>).
Conclusions

This study demonstrates that memory associated with a probe has multiple effects on the ERPs in CIT paradigms (N2, N400, P3b, and LPC), and the exact pattern of each effect depends upon the type of memory. <sentence_start/>Here, these effects are broadly consistent with the known properties of semantic and episodic memory systems, as assessed using ERPs. <sentence_start/>Documenting and examining these ERP effects is necessary to understand fully the neural basis of the processes engaged during CIT and related paradigms. <sentence_start/>For practical applications, analysis methods may be fine-tuned to detect concealed information depending on the associated memory type: For semantic probes, the focus should be the frontal N2, centroparietal N400, and parietal P3b, and for episodic probes the focus should be the P3b, and the LPC. <sentence_start/>Further, using longer sessions with more trials can efficiently improve signal-to-noise ratio because ERP CIT effects exhibited no signs of habituation or fatigue.

Altogether, the findings indicate that the frontal N2, centroparietal N400, and P3b are especially sensitive to information stored in knowledge and semantic memory systems of the neocortex, whereas the LPC is especially sensitive to information stored in the episodic memory system that depends on the hippocampus and adjacent cortical structures of the mediotemporal lobe. <sentence_start/>This conclusion highlights that clearly defining, manipulating, and considering the type of memory that may be concealed may be important for accurate detection of concealed information. <sentence_start/>Future CIT studies will need to consider carefully the semantic and episodic memory associated with each item, as well as how this interacts with task and experimental context. <sentence_start/>For example, if the goal is to reveal concealed episodic memory, then the semantic memory associated with each episodic item may need to be equated or specifically manipulated to separate out the semantic from episodic contributions. <sentence_start/>The present memory manipulation essentially orients subjects to focus on one memory system over another because the semantic and episodic probes that determined the memory system (i.e., semantic vs. episodic) for retrieval were presented in separate blocks of trials; participants did not have to discriminate between semantic and episodic probes directly. <sentence_start/>The strength of this approach is that it parallels the methods of memory research. <sentence_start/>Semantic memory experiments would involve asking subjects to report if the item exists in the real world, the meaning of a stimulus, or to categorize or name it, and items would differ in how well they are known (i.e., how well semantic memory is activated), akin to the semantic probe and irrelevants in this CIT paradigm. <sentence_start/>Episodic memory experiments would involve asking subjects to report whether the item is familiar from a prior study experience and/or to recollect associated information from that study experience, and familiar items would be mixed with unfamiliar items that had not been studied, akin to the episodic probe and irrelevants in this CIT paradigm. <sentence_start/>The present experiment was a first attempt at teasing apart semantic and episodic memory contributions to the CIT. <sentence_start/>However, here, as in the real world, items will usually activate both semantic and episodic memory to some extent. <sentence_start/>This mix needs to be carefully documented in CIT paradigms and, more broadly, in deception research.
